newsitem.title: USA: AMTRAK TRAIN DERAILS IN ARIZONA, 121 PEOPLE HURT.
newsitem.headline: AMTRAK TRAIN DERAILS IN ARIZONA, 121 PEOPLE HURT.

text.p: An Amtrak passenger train carrying mostly vacationers derailed while crossing a buckled bridge in northwestern Arizona on Saturday, injuring 121 passengers.

The train, Amtrak's Southwest Chief bound for Chicago, went off the Burlington Northern-Sante Fe tracks about 13 miles (21 km) east of Kingman, said Jon Poston, a state Corporation Commission spokesman.
Officials said none of the 121 people hurt in the accident had life-threatening injuries. They were treated at local hospitals.

"Many of them were what we would call walking wounded," Kingman Regional Medical Center spokesman Brian Turney said. "Their injuries are not what we would call life-threatening at this point." Erroneous early reports from railroad dispatchers indicated at least eight people were killed in the crash, but local officials said they had searched the wreckage and found no fatalities.
Mohave County Sheriff's spokeswoman Jody Schanaman said a car-by-car search revealed all 301 passengers were accounted for.
"We are aware of no life-threatening injuries," said Deborah Hare, an Amtrak spokeswoman in Chicago.
She said the train's manifest listed 307 passengers and 18 crew, but authorities said it was not clear if all those who had reserved a seat had boarded the train.
"I basically felt a couple of jolts and I was on the floor," one passenger told reporters. "The train was off the tracks after that."
Local authorities said the train tracks were heavily used and train traffic was backed up for several miles because of the derailment. It was unclear when the tracks would be repaired for travel.

The four-locomotive, 16-car train was traveling at 88 mph (142 kph) when it struck a bridge that had been buckled by a severe storm that passed through the area earlier in the evening, officials said.

National Transportation Safety Board Chairman James Hall, speaking to reporters in Washington before leaving for Arizona with an investigative team, said that was the authorized speed for trains passing through that stretch of open desert.
Hare said all of the train cars and three of the four locomotives derailed, but all remained upright and in line.
A passenger said he knew instantly what had occurred when he woke up in a sleeping car in the rear of the train.
"I felt the brakes really go on rapidly and then bumping," he told a reporter. "I knew we were on the ground and the cars had derailed.
All of the cars just about derailed off the train. None of them are on their side, but they tore the tracks up pretty good."
The train left Los Angeles on Friday night en route to Chicago.
The train stopped in Kingman and had been scheduled to make another stop in Flagstaff, Arizona. The accident occurred about 5 a.m. PDT (8 a.m. EDT/1200 GMT).
Kingman is about 110 miles (180 km) southeast of Las Vegas.
Officials said the area had been buffeted by high winds and heavy rains, causing normally dry river beds to be swollen with water. Rescue crews needed 4-wheel-drive vehicles to get to the train.

The derailment was the second major train crash in nearly two years in Arizona. Amtrak's Sunset Limited train derailed in October 1995 in a remote desert area of Arizona. One person was killed and 65 were reported injured.
Authorities said the tracks had been tampered with in that incident.
The most recent Amtrak derailment was Jan. 13 when a train en route to Seattle from Chicago derailed in Wyoming, injuring eight passengers.

The Southwest Chief provides the fastest rail link between Southern California and the Midwest, with direct connections to Santa Fe, New Mexico, and the Grand Canyon. A Native American Guide is on board the train between Albuquerque and Gallup, New Mexico.
